while general VQA datasets like VQA v2 [10], GQA [12], and Vibe-Eval [29] contain some number-based questions, they are not systematically focused on challenging object enumeration.
A unique and critical aspect of our data collection protocol is that the ground truth (GT) count for each image was established in situ, at the moment of image capture.
The 1,528 QA pairs were generated through a semi-automated procedure where we used the Gemini 2.5 Flash model to formulate natural language questions based on the GT counts.
each image was manually assigned by the author(s) to one of ten predefined categories that cover a broad range of everyday contexts, from kitchen scenes to outdoor environments
Our evaluation focuses on prominent, general-purpose MLLMs rather than specialized counting frameworks.
the goal of CountQA is not to benchmark the state-of-the-art in specialized counting, but to probe the emergent capabilities of generalist models.
We frame the counting task as a regression problem, where the desired output for each question is a single integer.
The primary metric for our evaluation is Exact Match (EM), which measures the percentage of predictions where the final extracted number is identical to the ground truth integer.
answer is considered correct under RA@5% or RA@10% if the predicted count falls within 5% or 10% of the ground truth value, respectively.
To ensure deterministic and fact-based responses, the generation temperature for all models was set to 0.
if an output was not a raw integer, we used Gemini 2.5 Flash as a rewriter LLM to extract the first numerical value from the verbose text.
Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves 60.3% EM, yet still fails on nearly 40% of these simple prompts.
For scenes with over 50 objects, the top model's accuracy falls to just 13.9%, and most other models are in the single digits.
our 'cluttered' scenes have a lower average object count (11.5) than our 'focused' scenes (15.7).
several top-tier models, including OpenAI o4-mini and Qwen VL Max, paradoxically performed slightly better.
The core problem appears to be a pipeline that is heavily optimized for semantic understanding at the cost of fine-grained perceptual accuracy.
First, the dataset's geographic and cultural scope is inherently linked to the environments of the author(s) who collected the images.
Second, there is a deliberate trade-off in our dataset design between scale and annotation quality.
the scope of the questions in CountQA is focused primarily on direct enumeration ("How many X?") and simple compositional counting ("How many X and Y?").

The results highlight the challenging nature of the dataset, with the top-performing model achieving 42.93% EM.
For the marshmallow example, a significant portion of the models, including several powerful open-source systems, produce off-by-one errors.
when tasked with counting a pile of 14 almonds, the best models provide answers near the ground truth, such as Gemini 2.5 Pro's prediction of 15.
In an example requiring the count of 15 jackets in a cluttered pile, nearly every model fails, most by a significant margin.
When asked to count "how many white hexagons" from a tiled surface or "red thumb pins" on a board, the error rates are extremely high across almost all models.
